report: Conclusion: the claim is **supported, with caveats**. The pivotal evidence is the NCIC CTG MAP.3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 4,560 postmenopausal women at moderately increased risk. At median 35 months, invasive breast cancer occurred in 11 women on exemestane 25 mg/day versus 32 on placebo: annual incidence 0.19% vs 0.55%, hazard ratio 0.35 (95% CI 0.18–0.70), i.e. about a 65% relative reduction but only ~0.36 percentage-point absolute reduction over ~3 years; invasive plus DCIS was also lower (HR 0.47). NCI summarizes the same finding as a substantial risk reduction in high-risk postmenopausal women. Guidelines reflect this: USPSTF gives a **B recommendation** to offer aromatase inhibitors to women at increased breast-cancer risk and low risk of medication harms. Caveats: MAP.3 showed prevention of incidence, not proven mortality benefit, with limited follow-up. Main-trial fractures were not increased at 35 months, but a nested substudy found worsened age-related bone loss, so bone monitoring and individualized risk–benefit discussion matter. Sources: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507 ; https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk ; https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction ; https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanonc/article/PIIS1470-2045(11)70389-8/abstract
